analysis.research_question_and_background: Uzbekistan continues to experience a significant burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection despite nationwide vaccination since 1998, and regional variation in disease distribution and transmission dynamics remains poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide cross-sectional study was conducted in Uzbekistan from July 2022 to June 2024, enrolling 10,552 adults selected via stratified random sampling from a parent cohort of 1,048,575 individuals across seven regions.
analysis.methods: Serological testing included hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc), and viral RNA detection, with multivariate logistic regression used to identify independent risk factors for HBV infection.
analysis.main_results: Overall HBsAg prevalence was 4.7% (95% CI: 4.3–5.1%), with geographic heterogeneity ranging from 3.2% in Tashkent to 6.3% in Bukhara; 68.1% of HBsAg-positive individuals had detectable HBV DNA, and 12.7% had HDV superinfection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights persistent HBV burden with notable regional clustering and identifies distinct transmission pathways for HDV superinfection, including a specific association with sharing personal hygiene items (aOR 2.34, 95% CI: 1.16–4.74; P = 0.02).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support intensified screening and treatment of unvaccinated adults and targeted household-level prevention measures, particularly for HDV transmission, to advance hepatitis elimination efforts in Uzbekistan.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and reliance on serological markers may underestimate occult HBV infection; however, the large, geographically stratified sample and robust statistical methods strengthen the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This nationwide cross-sectional study in Uzbekistan assessed the burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection among 10,552 adults from July 2022 to June 2024, using stratified random sampling from a parent cohort of over one million individuals. Serological testing revealed an overall HBsAg prevalence of 4.7%, with significant regional variation (3.2% in Tashkent to 6.3% in Bukhara). Among HBsAg-positive participants, 68.1% had detectable HBV DNA, and 12.7% had hepatitis D virus (HDV) superinfection. Multivariate analysis identified female sex as protective against chronic HBsAg carriage, while married status, healthcare exposures, and body piercings correlated with increased anti-HBc positivity. Notably, sharing personal hygiene items was specifically associated with HDV superinfection (aOR 2.34, 95% CI: 1.16–4.74; P = 0.02), suggesting distinct transmission pathways for HDV. The study underscores the need for intensified screening and targeted interventions, including household-level prevention, to address persistent HBV burden and HDV superinfection in Uzbekistan.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) worldwide, yet diagnostic tools for HBV-associated HCC require further optimization. The study aimed to develop a diagnostic model tailored for HBV-associated HCC to address gaps in current diagnostic performance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A diagnostic model (GADA) was developed and validated using data from 2190 patients with HBV-related liver diseases, including chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis, and HCC. External validation was performed on 20,908 patients across ten hospitals.
analysis.methods: The GADA model was created by omitting AFP-L3 from the GALAD model to improve accessibility, and its diagnostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Sensitivity and specificity were calculated to assess model performance.
analysis.main_results: In the modeling group, the GADA model achieved an AUC of 0.940 (95% CI, 0.927–0.952) with sensitivity 82.57% and specificity 91.53%, outperforming the original GALAD model (AUC 0.907). For early-stage HCC, the AUC was 0.858 in the modeling group and 0.868 in the internal validation group. External validation across 20,908 participants yielded an AUC of 0.919 with sensitivity 86.00% and specificity 81.88%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The GADA model demonstrated superior diagnostic performance compared to the GALAD model, particularly for early-stage HCC detection. The authors highlight its potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and reduce misdiagnosis rates in HBV-associated HCC.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The GADA model may improve early detection of HBV-related HCC, enabling timely intervention and better patient prognosis. Its robust validation across multiple centers supports potential clinical utility in HBV-endemic regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on retrospective data and hospital-based cohorts, which may limit generalizability. While external validation included a large sample, the model’s performance in diverse populations and real-world settings requires further evaluation.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed and validated the GADA model, a simplified diagnostic tool for HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by omitting AFP-L3 from the GALAD model. Using data from 2190 patients for model development and 20,908 patients across ten hospitals for validation, the GADA model achieved an AUC of 0.940 in the modeling group with sensitivity 82.57% and specificity 91.53%, outperforming the original GALAD model. For early-stage HCC, the AUC was 0.858 in the modeling group and 0.868 in the internal validation group. External validation yielded an AUC of 0.919 with sensitivity 86.00% and specificity 81.88%. The authors conclude that GADA shows exceptional promise for improving early HCC diagnosis in HBV-infected patients, with potential to enhance patient prognosis and treatment decisions.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the clinical significance of low-frequency Hepatitis B virus (HBV) variants in people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Botswana, where HBV genetic diversity may influence disease progression and treatment outcomes. The authors highlighted a knowledge gap regarding the detection and impact of these variants using traditional sequencing methods.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study utilized 104 HBV near-full-length sequences generated from PLHIV using next-generation sequencing (NGS). The sequences were analyzed to identify low-frequency variants and their potential clinical relevance.
analysis.methods: Low-frequency variants (5–50%) were filtered using an in-house bioinformatics suite (HBVgenomeR v5.9.7) and compared against known escape mutations, drug resistance mutations (DRMs), and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)-associated mutations reported at the consensus level. Unclassified variants were characterized by HBV open reading frames (ORFs) to determine mutation frequency per genomic region.
analysis.main_results: Six escape mutations were detected in 8/104 (7.7%) sequences, with surfaceN131T being the most prevalent (5/8). Six DRMs were observed in 30/104 (28.8%) sequences, with rtV173L being the most prevalent (21/30). Truncation mutations included rtA181T/sW172* and rtM204I/sW196L. Four HCC-associated variants were found in 8/104 (7.7%) sequences, with xP46S being the most prevalent (5/8). A total of 1152 unique uncharacterized variants were reported across all ORFs, present in 94/104 (90.4%) sequences, with the RNaseH domain having the highest burden (330/1152, 28.6%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence that deep sequencing identifies clinically significant HBV mutations below the 20% detection limit of traditional sequencing, which would otherwise go unreported. They emphasized the potential underreporting of mutational burden in PLHIV co-infected with HBV, underscoring the importance of deep sequencing for improved HBV/HIV management.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study suggests that deep sequencing could enhance surveillance and clinical decision-making for HBV in PLHIV by revealing low-frequency variants linked to drug resistance, immune escape, and HCC risk. This approach may inform tailored treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes in high-burden settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on a single cohort from Botswana, which may restrict generalizability to other populations. Additionally, the absence of functional validation for uncharacterized variants and the lack of longitudinal follow-up to assess clinical outcomes reduce the strength of causal inferences. The evidence is moderate due to these constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterized low-frequency Hepatitis B virus (HBV) variants in people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Botswana using next-generation sequencing (NGS). Among 104 near-full-length HBV sequences, six escape mutations were detected in 7.7% of samples, six drug resistance mutations (DRMs) in 28.8%, and four hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)-associated variants in 7.7%. Truncation mutations and 1152 unique uncharacterized variants were also identified, with the RNaseH domain showing the highest mutational burden. The authors highlight that deep sequencing reveals clinically significant mutations below the 20% detection threshold of traditional methods, which may otherwise go unreported. These findings underscore the potential underreporting of HBV mutational burden in PLHIV and emphasize the value of deep sequencing for improving HBV/HIV management. However, the study’s single-cohort design and lack of functional validation limit generalizability and causal inference, warranting cautious interpretation.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection represents a major global health burden with 240 million patients worldwide and limited therapeutic options. The study addresses the unmet need for more effective antiviral interventions by targeting the HBV capsid assembly process, which is critical for viral replication.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study characterizes the antiviral properties of the HBV capsid assembly modulator ALG-001075, the parent compound of pevifoscorvir sodium. It synthesizes preclinical data including cellular models, structural analyses, and in vivo efficacy studies in adeno-associated virus-HBV mice.
analysis.methods: ALG-001075 was evaluated for antiviral potency using cellular assays to determine EC50 and EC99.9 values. Structural characterization involved fluorescence quenching, electron microscopy, size-exclusion chromatography, immunofluorescent staining, NMR analysis, and solid-state NMR spectroscopy. In vivo efficacy was assessed in adeno-associated virus-HBV mice.
analysis.main_results: ALG-001075 demonstrated potent antiviral activity with EC50 values below 1 nM and an EC99.9 value of 22 nM. It induced the formation of empty viral particles without aberrant structures and produced a characteristic CAM-E fingerprint in solid-state NMR spectra. The compound showed activity against HBV genotypes A-J, nucleoside analogue-resistant strains, and most CAM-resistance mutations, except T33N, T33P, and V124G. In vivo, ALG-001075 achieved up to a 5 log10 reduction in circulating HBV DNA levels in mice.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings establish ALG-001075 as a highly potent and mechanistically distinct HBV capsid assembly modulator (CAM-E) with a favorable resistance profile. The atomic-resolution structural fingerprint and broad genotypic coverage represent novel contributions to HBV antiviral development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results support the clinical advancement of ALG-001075 as a promising therapeutic candidate for chronic HBV infection, particularly against resistant strains and diverse genotypes. Its potent antiviral activity and mechanistic specificity may inform future treatment strategies and resistance surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to preclinical and early clinical data summarized in the abstract, with no reported details on study design, sample sizes, or statistical analyses. The strength of evidence is moderate due to the absence of comprehensive methodological and outcome reporting.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterizes ALG-001075, a potent hepatitis B virus (HBV) capsid assembly modulator (CAM) and the parent compound of pevifoscorvir sodium, addressing the unmet need for improved HBV therapies. The compound exhibits exceptional antiviral potency with EC50 values below 1 nM and an EC99.9 of 22 nM, inducing the formation of empty viral particles without aberrant structures. Structural analyses via NMR and microscopy reveal a distinct CAM-E fingerprint at atomic resolution. ALG-001075 demonstrates broad activity across HBV genotypes A-J, nucleoside analogue-resistant strains, and most CAM-resistance mutations, with reduced efficacy against T33N, T33P, and V124G. In vivo efficacy is confirmed in adeno-associated virus-HBV mice, where the compound achieves up to a 5 log10 reduction in HBV DNA. These findings support its clinical development as a mechanistically novel and potent antiviral for chronic HBV infection.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) remains one of the most pervasive viral threats worldwide, posing a significant risk to millions. Due to the absence of proofreading activity during reverse transcription, HBV exhibits a high genetic variability.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study aimed to investigate the distribution of HBV genotypes among Iraqi patients and to characterize their molecular profiles. To date, ten distinct HBV genotypes have been identified globally, associated with varying disease outcomes, including progression to cirrhosis and carcinoma, as well as responses to antivirals.
analysis.methods: Therefore, a modified protocol was used to improve sequencing success rates in samples with low amplification yields.
analysis.main_results: HBV/D was predominant in the study cohort (100%). Subgenotypic analysis revealed that HBV/D1 accounts for the majority of cases (68%), followed by D3 (32%). Moreover, the analysis of antiviral resistance indicated that 47% (32/68) of HBV/D1 isolates exhibited drug resistance, with all resistant isolates showing mutations associated with Lamivudine resistance (100%), Entecavir intermediate/high resistance (81% and 19%, respectively), and Telbivudine (25%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings underscore the dominance of genotype D, particularly HBV/D1 among Iraqi patients. To our knowledge, this is the first local study to correlate genotypic variation with drug resistance and highlight the importance of continuous surveillance for antiviral resistance to guide effective treatment strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of continuous surveillance for antiviral resistance to guide effective treatment strategies. The dominance of genotype D, particularly HBV/D1, among Iraqi patients has significant implications for the management of HBV infection in the region.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations. The study provides a high confidence assessment based on the analysis of HBV genotypes and drug resistance mutations in Iraqi patients.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the distribution of HBV genotypes among Iraqi patients and characterized their molecular profiles. It found that HBV/D was predominant, with HBV/D1 accounting for 68% of cases. Antiviral resistance analysis revealed that 47% of HBV/D1 isolates exhibited drug resistance, with mutations associated with Lamivudine resistance (100%), Entecavir intermediate/high resistance (81% and 19%, respectively), and Telbivudine (25%). These findings underscore the dominance of genotype D in Iraq and highlight the need for continuous surveillance to guide treatment strategies. The study provides a high confidence assessment based on its focus on HBV genotypes and resistance mutations in the local population.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Occupational exposure to hepatitis B virus (HBV) places healthcare workers (HCWs) at elevated risk, yet vaccination coverage remains suboptimal despite the availability of a safe and effective vaccine. Volunteer HCWs face unique barriers such as financial constraints and are often overlooked in research, creating a knowledge gap about their vaccination status and determinants.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A national cross-sectional study was conducted among volunteer HCWs in Zambia using a self-administered semi-structured online questionnaire administered from October 3 to November 26, 2024. The study included 173 participants and aimed to assess HBV vaccination uptake and its predictors.
analysis.methods: Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics with R version 4.6.0 and Stata version 17, applying a two-sided p value threshold of less than 0.05 for statistical significance. A multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression model was used to identify independent predictors of vaccination uptake.
analysis.main_results: Among 173 participants, 51 (29.5%) reported being vaccinated; of these, 23 (45.1%) had received one dose, 4 (7.8%) two doses, and 24 (47.1%) at least three doses (fully vaccinated). Access to HBV vaccination programs during training was significantly associated with vaccination (p < 0.001), as was the availability of HBV testing services at the health facility (p = 0.006). Increasing age was also associated with higher odds of vaccination (p = 0.025), while gender and place of education were not independently associated after adjustment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights low HBV vaccination coverage among volunteer HCWs in Zambia and identifies institutional and demographic factors—vaccination programs during training, age, and on-site HBV testing services—as key determinants of uptake. This underscores the need for targeted interventions within training and facility-based prevention programs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that strengthening HBV vaccination programs during training and improving access to on-site testing services could substantially increase vaccination coverage among volunteer HCWs, thereby reducing occupational HBV infection risk in Zambia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and reliance on self-reported vaccination status may introduce recall bias. The sample size of 173 participants and single-country setting further constrain generalizability, warranting cautious interpretation of the evidence strength as moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study assessed hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination uptake and predictors among 173 volunteer healthcare workers (HCWs) in Zambia using an online questionnaire administered from October to November 2024. Only 29.5% reported vaccination, with 47.1% of vaccinated participants fully immunized. Access to vaccination programs during training (p < 0.001) and availability of HBV testing services at health facilities (p = 0.006) were independently associated with higher uptake, as was increasing age (p = 0.025). Gender and place of education showed no independent association. The authors conclude that HBV vaccination coverage among volunteer HCWs is low and recommend strengthening institutional prevention programs to improve uptake and reduce occupational risk.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) are a promising antiviral class for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but no simple method exists to estimate their in vivo antiviral effectiveness during clinical evaluation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study performed viral dynamics modeling of HBV RNA, HBV DNA, and ALT during phase I trials of two CAMs, vebicorvir and ABI-H2158, which inhibit pgRNA encapsidation.
analysis.methods: Viral dynamics modeling was used to fit intracellular and extracellular HBV RNA, HBV DNA, and ALT data, quantifying drug-induced inhibition of encapsidated pgRNA production as in vivo antiviral effectiveness.
analysis.main_results: The magnitude of the first phase of HBV RNA and HBV DNA decline was explicitly related to CAM effectiveness, and declines between baseline and day 14 of monotherapy predicted effectiveness.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that HBV RNA is a clinically relevant biomarker and that very short-term phase I trials can evaluate CAM effectiveness, potentially reducing resistance development risk.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest HBV RNA and HBV DNA declines during early monotherapy can inform dose selection and accelerate evaluation of new CAMs in phase I trials.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report sampling density constraints or validation in diverse HBV genotypes, limiting generalisability and precision of early-phase estimates.

analysis.summary_en: This study used viral dynamics modeling to quantify the in vivo antiviral effectiveness of two capsid assembly modulators (CAMs), vebicorvir and ABI-H2158, by fitting HBV RNA, HBV DNA, and ALT data from phase I trials. The magnitude of the first-phase decline in HBV RNA and HBV DNA directly reflected CAM effectiveness, and declines measured between baseline and day 14 of monotherapy predicted effectiveness. The authors propose HBV RNA as a clinically relevant biomarker and suggest that short-term phase I trials can reliably assess CAM effectiveness, potentially reducing resistance development risk. However, the evidence does not address sampling limitations or validation across HBV genotypes, which constrains generalisability.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Occult hepatitis B virus infection (OBI) persists despite undetectable hepatitis B surface antigen, and the genetic mechanisms underlying host control remain incompletely understood. The study aimed to identify human leukocyte antigen (HLA) determinants that influence susceptibility to OBI.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study performed high-resolution HLA genotyping and amino acid-based association analysis in a Chinese population of 239 OBI cases and 545 healthy controls.
analysis.methods: High-resolution HLA genotyping and amino acid-based association analysis were conducted to identify HLA class II alleles and structural residues associated with OBI.
analysis.main_results: The HLA class II allele DQB1*06:02 was identified as a protective signal against OBI, with conditional analysis confirming its independent effect. The DRB1*09:01~DQA1*03:02~DQB1*03:03 haplotype was associated with increased OBI risk. Position 119 in the HLA-DQB1 peptide-binding groove, specifically the phenylalanine variant encoded by DQB1*06:02, drove a substantial portion of the observed association.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings delineate both allele and amino acid level HLA determinants of OBI susceptibility, highlighting a key structural residue that may influence antigen presentation and immune clearance of HBV. This provides a refined genetic framework for understanding host-virus interactions in occult HBV persistence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that HLA-DQB1*06:02 and the phenylalanine variant at position 119 could inform genetic risk stratification and vaccine design strategies targeting occult HBV infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a single Chinese population, which may restrict generalisability to other ethnic groups. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on observational association without functional validation of the structural mechanism.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated host genetic determinants of occult hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection (OBI) by performing high-resolution HLA genotyping and amino acid-based association analysis in a Chinese cohort of 239 OBI cases and 545 healthy controls. The HLA class II allele DQB1*06:02 was identified as a protective factor against OBI, with its independent effect confirmed through conditional analysis. Conversely, the DRB1*09:01~DQA1*03:02~DQB1*03:03 haplotype was associated with increased OBI risk. Structural analysis revealed that position 119 in the HLA-DQB1 peptide-binding groove, specifically the phenylalanine variant encoded by DQB1*06:02, drove a substantial portion of the association. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that HLA-DQB1*06:02 and the phenylalanine variant at position 119 may influence antigen presentation and immune clearance of HBV, providing a refined genetic framework for understanding occult HBV persistence. The results suggest potential implications for genetic risk stratification and vaccine design, though the study's single-population design and observational nature limit generalisability and functional validation.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate how drug resistance mutations (DRMs) in the surface antigen of hepatitis B virus (HBV) affect the assembly and infectivity of hepatitis delta virus (HDV). The background highlights the importance of understanding these interactions to improve therapeutic strategies for HBV/HDV co-infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 30 DRMs in HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) selected by FDA-approved anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs. These DRMs were tested for their impact on HDV assembly and infectivity in a controlled experimental setting.
analysis.methods: The researchers examined the ability of DRM-bearing HBsAg variants to support HDV formation and secretion by analyzing HDV RNA genome levels and the fraction of HDV-infected cells. They also identified the specific regions of HBsAg where DRMs exerted their effects.
analysis.main_results: All DRM-bearing HBsAg variants supported HDV formation and secretion, but only 13/30 DRMs significantly reduced the yield of secreted HDV virions. Additionally, 23/30 DRMs greatly reduced HDV infectivity, with four causing a complete loss of infectivity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that DRMs in specific regions of HBsAg can inhibit HDV infectivity through direct and indirect mechanisms, altering virion attachment/entry, trafficking, and uncoating. They also identified transmembrane domains II, III, and IV as critical regulators of HDV infectivity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that anti-HBV drug treatments may influence HDV life cycle and reduce HDV spread/superinfection, potentially leading to a decrease in HDV-associated liver pathogenesis in chronically infected individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to an abstract-only analysis, and the evidence is based on experimental observations of DRM effects on HDV. The confidence in these findings is moderate due to the lack of detailed experimental data and broader clinical validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how drug resistance mutations (DRMs) in the surface antigen of hepatitis B virus (HBV) affect the assembly and infectivity of hepatitis delta virus (HDV). The research analyzed 30 DRMs selected by FDA-approved anti-HBV drugs and found that while all DRM-bearing HBsAg variants supported HDV formation, only 13/30 DRMs significantly reduced HDV virion yield. Moreover, 23/30 DRMs greatly reduced HDV infectivity, with four causing complete loss of infectivity. The authors suggest that DRMs may alter HDV infectivity through direct and indirect mechanisms, affecting virion attachment, trafficking, and uncoating. They also identified transmembrane domains II, III, and IV of HBsAg as critical regulators of HDV infectivity. These findings highlight the potential of anti-HBV treatments to suppress HDV spread and reduce liver pathogenesis. However, the study is limited to abstract-only evidence, and the results need further experimental and clinical validation to establish their broader implications.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aims to refine patient selection for achieving a functional cure in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) by validating the GOLDEN prediction model, which uses quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) kinetics to identify optimal candidates for therapy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a prospective multicentre observational cohort study enrolling 300 NA-experienced patients with CHB from 22 centres in China. Patients are stratified into two groups based on the predictive index (Pi) calculated from pre-treatment qHBsAg dynamics: favourable (Pi>0.15, n=150) and unfavourable candidates (Pi≤0.15, n=150).
analysis.methods: The study will use a combination therapy of Peg-IFN α-2b plus ongoing nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) for all patients over 48 weeks. Between-group comparisons will be conducted using the χ2 or Fisher's exact test.
analysis.main_results: The primary endpoint is the HBsAg clearance rate at week 48, with clearance defined as HBsAg loss at any time during the treatment period. The sample size provides 80% power to detect a significant difference between the assumed clearance rates (35% vs 20%, favourable vs unfavourable group).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The GOLDEN model, based on sequential changes in qHBsAg, accurately predicts HBsAg loss in patients with CHB receiving NA therapy. The study will explore establishing novel predictive models using this framework alongside other baseline indicators.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more effective strategies for selecting patients for combination therapy, potentially improving the likelihood of achieving a functional cure in chronic hepatitis B.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single predictive model and does not include long-term follow-up data. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on a prospective observational design with a defined sample size and statistical analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study protocol outlines a prospective multicentre observational cohort study aimed at validating the GOLDEN prediction model for identifying optimal candidates for a functional cure in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy combined with pegylated interferon α-2b (Peg-IFN α-2b). The study will enrol 300 NA-experienced patients with CHB from 22 centres in China, stratified into favourable (Pi>0.15) and unfavourable (Pi≤0.15) groups based on pre-treatment quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) dynamics. The primary endpoint is HBsAg clearance at week 48, with secondary endpoints including HBsAg seroconversion and sustained clearance rates. The study will use χ2 or Fisher's exact tests for between-group comparisons and aims to provide 80% power to detect a significant difference between clearance rates (35% vs 20%). The GOLDEN model, which uses sequential qHBsAg changes, is interpreted as accurately predicting HBsAg loss in CHB patients on NA therapy. The findings may inform improved patient selection strategies for combination therapy. However, the study is limited to a single model and lacks long-term follow-up data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the impact of immune delay and noise on HBV infection dynamics in vivo, as these factors are ubiquitous in the evolution of HBV infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A stochastic HBV infection dynamic model was proposed to investigate the interaction effects of interval delay and white noise during the immune phase. The model focuses on human hepatitis B virus infection and its in vivo dynamics.
analysis.methods: Global existence, nonnegativity, and boundedness of the solutions were obtained through mathematical analysis. The stochastic reproduction number was derived as a threshold for determining viral extinction or persistence within-host. Numerical simulations using time-series analysis were conducted to confirm the existence of stochastic periodicity.
analysis.main_results: The stability conditions for the first and second moments were established. Numerical simulations confirmed the existence of stochastic periodicity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that noise induces an earlier onset of stochastic periodicity compared to the deterministic model. This finding highlights the role of immune noise in shaping HBV infection dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more accurate models for HBV infection dynamics, which may aid in understanding the mechanisms of viral persistence and the design of targeted interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a mathematical model and does not involve empirical data. The evidence is abstract-only, and the confidence in the findings is moderate due to the lack of direct experimental validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the dynamics of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in vivo, focusing on the effects of immune delay and noise. A stochastic model was developed to analyze the interaction of interval delay and white noise during the immune phase. The model established global existence, nonnegativity, and boundedness of solutions, derived a stochastic reproduction number as a threshold for viral extinction or persistence, and confirmed the existence of stochastic periodicity through numerical simulations. The authors interpreted that immune noise leads to an earlier onset of stochastic periodicity compared to deterministic models, suggesting that noise plays a significant role in HBV infection dynamics. The findings have implications for improving models of HBV infection and understanding viral persistence mechanisms. However, the study is based on a mathematical model without empirical data, limiting the confidence in its conclusions to a moderate level.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for a deeper understanding of within-host dynamics during hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, particularly the mechanisms underlying viral persistence and spread across spatially distinct liver regions. It highlights the gap in mathematical modeling of HBV infection across multiple liver patches and frames the objective to analyze such dynamics with unidirectional viral transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors propose and analyze a mathematical model describing two-patch within-host HBV infection dynamics with unidirectional viral spread from patch-1 to patch-2. The model conceptualizes interactions among six compartments: uninfected hepatocytes, infected hepatocytes, and free HBV particles in each of the two patches.
analysis.methods: The study employs a mathematical modeling approach to analyze HBV infection dynamics, including the calculation of basic reproduction numbers (R1 and R2) for each patch using the next generation method. Global stability of equilibrium points is examined through rigorous proofs using Lyapunov functions and LaSalle’s invariance principle.
analysis.main_results: The basic reproduction numbers in patch-1 (R1) and patch-2 (R2) are calculated using the next generation method. Global stability of all equilibrium points is rigorously examined using Lyapunov functions and LaSalle’s invariance principle.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as demonstrating the feasibility of modeling HBV within-host dynamics across spatially distinct liver regions and identifying conditions for viral persistence or clearance. The novelty lies in the rigorous mathematical analysis of global stability and the explicit consideration of unidirectional viral transmission between patches.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted antiviral strategies by identifying key parameters influencing viral persistence, potentially guiding treatment optimization for chronic HBV infection. The model may also contribute to understanding the spatial heterogeneity of HBV infection within the liver.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to abstract-level descriptions and lacks empirical validation or clinical data, which constrains the strength of the conclusions. The study relies solely on mathematical modeling and theoretical analysis, without experimental or observational corroboration.

analysis.summary_en: This study proposes a two-patch mathematical model to analyze within-host hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection dynamics with unidirectional viral spread from one liver region to another. The model includes six compartments representing uninfected hepatocytes, infected hepatocytes, and free HBV particles in each patch. Using the next generation method, the authors calculate basic reproduction numbers for each patch and rigorously examine global stability of equilibrium points via Lyapunov functions and LaSalle’s invariance principle. The work highlights the feasibility of modeling spatial HBV dynamics and identifies conditions for viral persistence or clearance. While mathematically rigorous, the study is limited to theoretical analysis without empirical validation, which constrains the strength of its conclusions and public health implications.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chronic hepatitis B remains difficult to monitor because conventional serum markers reflect both infectious and non-infectious viral components. The study was needed to determine whether the Hepatitis B surface antigen glycan isomer (HBsAgGi)—which marks O-glycosylated M-HBsAg on infectious Dane particles—can serve as a more specific circulating biomarker for intrahepatic cccDNA activity and antiviral response.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cohort of 73 individuals with chronic genotype C HBV infection was enrolled. Serum HBsAgGi, HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA, HBV RNA and HBcrAg were quantified. Intrahepatic cccDNA and HBV RNA were measured in liver biopsy specimens from 16 patients, and HBcrAg was measured in 28 patients.
analysis.methods: Serum concentrations of HBsAgGi and other markers were measured, and intrahepatic cccDNA and HBV RNA loads were determined from liver biopsies. Correlations between serum HBsAgGi and intrahepatic markers were analyzed. ROC curve analysis assessed the discriminative ability of candidate biomarkers in predicting virological response after 48 weeks of nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy in 18 patients.
analysis.main_results: Serum HBsAgGi showed significant positive correlations with intrahepatic cccDNA (r = 0.7172, P < 0.01), HBV RNA (r = 0.7879, P < 0.01), and the RNA/cccDNA ratio (r = 0.5840, P < 0.05), outperforming conventional serum markers. HBsAgGi also correlated strongly with serum HBcrAg (r = 0.5361, P < 0.01) in 28 patients. Baseline HBsAgGi predicted virological response with an AUC of 0.9538.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret HBsAgGi as an emerging, minimally invasive serum indicator that more closely reflects intrahepatic cccDNA loads and transcriptional activity than conventional markers. They highlight its superior predictive utility for treatment response in this cohort.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest HBsAgGi could improve monitoring of cccDNA activity and early prediction of antiviral response in chronic hepatitis B, potentially guiding treatment decisions and follow-up strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its modest sample size, single-cohort design, and reliance on liver biopsy data from only 16 patients, which constrains generalizability. Evidence strength is assessed as moderate pending validation in larger, multi-center cohorts.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated whether the Hepatitis B surface antigen glycan isomer (HBsAgGi) can serve as a minimally invasive biomarker for intrahepatic cccDNA activity and antiviral response in chronic hepatitis B. In 73 patients with chronic genotype C HBV infection, serum HBsAgGi showed stronger correlations with intrahepatic cccDNA (r = 0.7172, P < 0.01) and HBV RNA (r = 0.7879, P < 0.01) than conventional markers, and predicted virological response with an AUC of 0.9538 after 48 weeks of nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy. HBsAgGi also correlated with serum HBcrAg (r = 0.5361, P < 0.01) in 28 patients. The authors conclude that HBsAgGi is a promising serum indicator for monitoring cccDNA activity and predicting treatment response, though the evidence is limited by small sample size and single-cohort design.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the unresolved risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection or reactivation in people with HIV (PWH) after switching to antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens lacking anti-HBV activity, particularly in settings where universal HBV vaccination has been recently implemented.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted among PWH receiving ART without tenofovir, lamivudine, or emtricitabine between January 2005 and March 2026, with participants followed during periods off anti-HBV–active drugs.
analysis.methods: HBV serological status at baseline was classified, and incident HBV infection and reactivation were defined using serological and virological criteria during follow-up periods without anti-HBV–active ART components.
analysis.main_results: Among 166 PWH with 716 person-years of follow-up, five HBV-related events occurred: two incident HBV infections in HBV-naïve individuals and three HBV reactivations (two suspected, one confirmed), yielding an overall incidence rate of 0.70 per 100 person-years and 1.28 per 100 person-years in anti-HBs–negative individuals.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that the risk of HBV infection and reactivation becomes apparent in PWH on ART without anti-HBV activity, particularly among those without anti-HBs, including those with isolated anti-HBc, in settings with limited impact of universal HBV vaccination.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the need for continued HBV surveillance and consideration of anti-HBV–active ART in PWH, especially in populations with waning vaccine-induced immunity or isolated anti-HBc serology.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The retrospective single-center design, small number of events, and lack of adjustment for potential confounders limit causal inference and generalizability, warranting cautious interpretation of the moderate-strength evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This single-center retrospective cohort study in Japan evaluated the risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and reactivation in 166 people with HIV (PWH) after switching to antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens without anti-HBV activity between 2005 and 2026. Over 716 person-years of follow-up, five HBV-related events occurred, including two incident infections and three reactivations, with an overall incidence rate of 0.70 per 100 person-years and 1.28 per 100 person-years in anti-HBs–negative individuals. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly lower event-free survival in anti-HBs–negative individuals (log-rank p = 0.0084). The authors concluded that HBV infection and reactivation risks become apparent in PWH on ART without anti-HBV activity, particularly among those without anti-HBs or with isolated anti-HBc, especially where universal HBV vaccination has had limited impact. The study underscores the need for targeted HBV surveillance and consideration of anti-HBV–active ART in this population.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major transfusion-transmissible infection in sub-Saharan Africa. Blood donor surveillance is essential for maintaining a safe blood supply.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional retrospective study was conducted among 140 blood donors screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). Donors were predominantly male (75.0%), aged 18–22 years (42.1%), urban residents (78.6%), with secondary (52.9%) or tertiary education (35.9%).
analysis.methods: Associations between HBV seropositivity and donor characteristics were analyzed using chi-square tests, while significant variables were further assessed using multivariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: The overall HBV prevalence was 10.0% (14/140). HBV prevalence was higher among males (10.5%) than females (8.6%), though not statistically significant (p=0.735). Rural donors recorded significantly higher prevalence (20.0%) compared to urban donors (7.3%; p=0.038). HBV infection was most common among donors with primary education (25.0%; p=0.047). Behavioural factors showed strong associations: history of surgery/transfusion (25.0%; p=0.016), tattooing/scarification (33.3%; p=0.001), and multiple sexual partners (23.3%; p=0.007). None of the vaccinated donors were HBsAg-positive (0.0%; p=0.009).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Multivariate analysis identified tattooing/scarification (AOR=6.8; p=0.004), multiple sexual partners (AOR=4.1; p=0.023), and vaccination status (AOR=0.001; p=0.002) as independent predictors of HBV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: HBV prevalence among UTH blood donors remains substantial. Strengthened HBV vaccination, community-level health education, and rigorous donor risk assessment are recommended for improving blood safety.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the prevalence of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection among blood donors at the University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka, Zambia. A cross-sectional retrospective study was conducted on 140 donors, with data extracted from routine blood bank records. The overall HBV prevalence was 10.0%, with higher rates observed among rural donors (20.0%) and those with primary education (25.0%). Behavioral factors such as history of surgery/transfusion, tattooing/scarification, and multiple sexual partners were strongly associated with HBV infection. Vaccination status was found to be a protective factor, as none of the vaccinated donors were HBsAg-positive. The study highlights the importance of targeted vaccination, health education, and donor risk assessment to enhance blood safety. The findings are based on abstract-only evidence, and the study design does not include detailed limitations.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Chronic Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection imposes a substantial global health burden, yet no curative therapy exists, highlighting a critical knowledge gap in understanding host-virus interactions that could reveal therapeutic targets.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examined HBV entry, replication, viral particle envelopment, and secretion in hepatic cells with depleted Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) expression or treated with NPC1 inhibitors, focusing on mechanistic regulation of the EGFR receptor.
analysis.methods: Cells were genetically depleted of NPC1 or exposed to FDA-approved NPC1 inhibitors to assess effects on HBV infection steps and EGFR levels, with mechanistic evaluation of endocytic trafficking and receptor degradation.
analysis.main_results: Both genetic depletion and pharmacological inhibition of NPC1 impaired early HBV infection and significantly reduced EGFR levels and its intracellular distribution in hepatic cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors propose that NPC1 regulates HBV infection by maintaining EGFR at the plasma membrane, identifying a novel NPC1-EGFR regulatory axis with potential dual therapeutic implications for antiviral and anticancer strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest NPC1 and EGFR could serve as targets for developing therapies against HBV infection and associated hepatocellular carcinoma, warranting further translational research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to in vitro hepatic cell models and lacks in vivo validation or clinical data, indicating moderate strength and the need for broader experimental confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated how Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) protein regulates Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in hepatic cells by modulating Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) stability. The authors demonstrated that both genetic depletion and pharmacological inhibition of NPC1 impaired early HBV infection steps and reduced EGFR levels and intracellular distribution. Mechanistically, NPC1 inhibition enhanced EGFR endocytic trafficking and lysosomal degradation. The work identifies a novel NPC1-EGFR regulatory axis with potential dual therapeutic implications for HBV infection and associated hepatocellular carcinoma. However, the evidence is confined to in vitro models and lacks in vivo or clinical validation, indicating moderate strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess knowledge and perceptions regarding hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, transmission, occupational risk, and vaccination status among dental students and house officers in Abbottabad. This is important due to the potential occupational exposure of dental professionals to HBV.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted among dental students and house officers/interns at the Dental Section, Ayub Medical Complex, Abbottabad. The study included 121 participants, with 86 (71.1%) being female and 48 (39.7%) aged 21–23 years.
analysis.methods: Data were collected through a structured, self-administered paper-based questionnaire and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 24. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages.
analysis.main_results: Sixty-nine (57.0%) participants had received at least one HBV vaccine dose, while 52 (43.0%) were unvaccinated. Among vaccinated participants, 28 (40.6%) had received two doses, 26 (37.7%) one dose, and 15 (21.7%) three doses. Body fluids (107, 88.4%) and blood (90, 74.4%) were the most frequently identified transmission routes. Seventy-three (60.3%) participants perceived a high occupational risk.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that awareness of HBV infection and vaccination was generally high, but vaccination uptake and completion of the recommended three-dose schedule were inadequate. This study highlights the need for improved vaccination programs among dental trainees.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted educational interventions and vaccination campaigns to improve occupational protection among dental professionals, particularly in regions with high HBV prevalence.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used purposive non-probability sampling, which may introduce selection bias. Additionally, no significant gender differences were observed across the assessed knowledge, perception, and vaccination variables (all p>0.05). The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study assessed the level of awareness and knowledge of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and vaccination among dental students and house officers in Abbottabad. The study found that while awareness was generally high, vaccination uptake and completion of the three-dose schedule were inadequate. Body fluids and blood were identified as the most common transmission routes, and most participants perceived a high occupational risk. The authors suggest that strengthening HBV education and vaccination programs before clinical training may improve occupational protection. However, the study's use of purposive non-probability sampling introduces potential bias, and no significant gender differences were observed. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a significant transfusion-transmissible infection, posing a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. Understanding the socio-demographic profile of blood donors is essential to ensure blood safety and guide targeted interventions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted among voluntary blood donors at Saint Joseph Hospital, Monrovia, from January to December 2024. A total of 1,574 blood donors were screened, with 1,446 (91.8%) qualifying for donation.
analysis.methods: Socio-demographic data, including age, sex, education level, and occupation, were collected via structured questionnaires. Blood samples were screened for HBV using standard serological methods. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize donor characteristics, and HBV prevalence was calculated monthly.
analysis.main_results: Male donors predominated, ranging from 59 (94%) in January to 138 (92%) in December, while females accounted for 4 (6.3%) to 12 (8%). The majority of donors were aged 18–35 years (67–71%), followed by 36–45 years (25–39%) and 46–60 years (6–21%). Most donors had secondary education or higher (69–79%). Employed donors accounted for 55–71%, self-employed 19–27%, and students 8–18%. HBV prevalence among tested donors increased over the year, starting at 14.3% in January (1/7), rising to 35.7% in June and October (5/14), and peaking at 37.5% in December (6/16).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as highlighting the high and increasing prevalence of HBV among blood donors, which underscores the need for targeted public health education and interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted public health education and interventions to reduce HBV transmission through blood donations, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa where HBV poses a significant public health challenge.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data, which may introduce bias. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of longitudinal follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study assessed the prevalence and distribution of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection among blood donors at Saint Joseph Hospital, Monrovia, from January to December 2024. The study found that male donors predominated, with the majority aged 18–35 years and having secondary education or higher. HBV prevalence increased throughout the year, peaking at 37.5% in December. The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the urgent need for strengthened screening and public health education to reduce transfusion-transmitted infections. The study's limitations include its cross-sectional design and potential for self-reporting bias, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui faktor-faktor yang memengaruhi pemberian imunisasi Hepatitis B pada bayi baru lahir di Ruang Perinatologi Rumah Sakit Avicenna Bireuen.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Penelitian menggunakan desain analitik dengan pendekatan cross sectional. Populasi dan sampel berjumlah 45 ibu yang memiliki bayi baru lahir dengan teknik total sampling.
analysis.methods: Pengumpulan data menggunakan kuesioner dan dilaksanakan pada 1–14 Agustus 2024.
analysis.main_results: Hasil penelitian menunjukkan adanya pengaruh pengetahuan ibu (p=0,001), sikap ibu (p=0,003), dukungan keluarga (p=0,001), dan stres (p=0,017) terhadap pemberian imunisasi Hepatitis B pada bayi baru lahir (α=0,05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Penelitian ini menemukan bahwa pengetahuan, sikap, dukungan keluarga, dan tingkat stres ibu berpengaruh signifikan terhadap keputusan pemberian imunisasi Hepatitis B pada bayi baru lahir.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Temuan ini dapat memberikan wawasan untuk meningkatkan upaya edukasi dan intervensi terhadap ibu hamil dan keluarga dalam meningkatkan penerimaan imunisasi Hepatitis B pada bayi baru lahir.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Penelitian ini memiliki desain cross-sectional yang membatasi kemampuan untuk menetapkan hubungan sebab-akibat, dan hanya melibatkan 45 responden, sehingga hasilnya memiliki kekuatan bukti yang moderat.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify factors influencing the administration of Hepatitis B vaccine to newborns in the Perinatology Unit of Avicenna Bireuen Hospital. It employed a cross-sectional analytical design, collecting data from 45 mothers using a questionnaire between August 1–14, 2024. The results showed that maternal knowledge (p=0.001), attitude (p=0.003), family support (p=0.001), and stress (p=0.017) significantly affected the decision to administer the Hepatitis B vaccine to newborns (α=0.05). The findings suggest that improving maternal education and addressing stress and attitudes could enhance vaccine uptake. However, the study's cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the moderate sample size suggests the evidence strength is limited.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the incidence of liver cancer and decompensated cirrhosis among individuals with hepatitis B and C in Tasmania, as liver cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related death globally and has seen rising incidence and mortality rates in Australia over the past three decades.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective population-based study was conducted using linked datasets, including all individuals with a notification for hepatitis B and/or C in Tasmania from 1995 to 2022. Cases were linked to the Tasmanian Cancer Register and admitted patient data from Tasmanian public hospitals.
analysis.methods: The study used a retrospective population-based design, linking hepatitis B and C notifications to cancer and hospital admission records. Incidence rates per 1,000 person-years were calculated for liver cancer and decompensated cirrhosis.
analysis.main_results: Between 1995 and 2022, 1,280 hepatitis B (55.5% male) and 6,658 hepatitis C (64.3% male) notifications were recorded. A total of 145 liver cancer registrations and 270 decompensated cirrhosis-related admissions were observed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as highlighting the burden of liver-related complications among individuals with hepatitis B and C in Tasmania, noting a trend towards higher incidence rates over the study period.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest the importance of strengthening testing, treatment uptake, and long-term monitoring to reduce the burden of advanced liver disease in this regional setting.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The number of liver-related outcomes was relatively low, limiting the ability to conduct more detailed analyses, and observed trends should be interpreted cautiously due to potential changes in population characteristics, surveillance, and healthcare engagement.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the incidence of liver cancer and decompensated cirrhosis among individuals with hepatitis B and C in Tasmania, using linked administrative datasets. It found that 1,280 hepatitis B and 6,658 hepatitis C notifications were recorded between 1995 and 2022, with 145 liver cancer registrations and 270 decompensated cirrhosis-related admissions observed. Incidence rates were 5.39 per 1,000 person-years for liver cancer among hepatitis B cases and 3.00 per 1,000 person-years for decompensated cirrhosis. For hepatitis C, the rates were 2.33 for liver cancer and 5.02 for decompensated cirrhosis. The authors noted a trend towards higher incidence rates over time but emphasized the need for cautious interpretation due to potential changes in population characteristics and healthcare engagement. They concluded that these findings highlight the burden of liver-related complications in Tasmania and underscore the importance of improving testing, treatment, and monitoring to address advanced liver disease.

analysis.scope_and_question: Chronic hepatitis D represents the most severe form of viral hepatitis and is associated with higher rates of advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma than hepatitis B monoinfection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: It is caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV), a defective RNA virus that requires co‐infection with hepatitis B (HBV) for hepatocyte entry and propagation.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Accurate prediction of liver disease sequelae and treatment response using currently available serological biomarkers remains challenging.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Establishing the role of these biomarkers in larger, ethnically diverse populations both on existing treatments and in the context of emerging antiviral therapies will be imperative going forward.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Peripheral biomarkers capable of risk stratifying patients with HDV, monitoring or predicting treatment response and elucidating the natural history of infection (including the complex relationship with HBV), would enable individualised care and early identification of those at greater risk of developing advanced liver disease.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on the challenges of using peripheral biomarkers to predict liver disease progression and treatment response in chronic hepatitis D. It highlights the need for more accurate biomarkers to enable individualized care and early identification of patients at risk of advanced liver disease. The review emphasizes the importance of studying these biomarkers in diverse populations and under various treatment contexts. The article also explores the potential clinical utility of novel biomarkers related to HBV activity, underscoring the complex relationship between HDV and HBV.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of an integrated antenatal care testing panel for accelerating the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B in Nigeria, as the World Health Organization pre-qualified such a panel in 2025.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A modeling study was conducted in Nigeria, considering 6.4 million women entering antenatal care annually, with a focus on current and projected future practices for testing and treatment.
analysis.methods: Deterministic and probabilistic models were constructed using Microsoft Excel and Python, incorporating parallel testing and treatment protocols for positive p24 antigen, calibrated with epidemiologic literature, product prices, and expert opinion.
analysis.main_results: The integrated testing panel would avert 562 of the current 3,299 vertical infections per 100,000 women in antenatal care, and avert 0.0656 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per woman at a net cost of US$7.55.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that the integrated ANC testing panel would be a valuable and cost-effective addition to antenatal care, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $115 per DALY averted, more favorable than Nigeria's historical average.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that implementing the integrated testing panel could improve surveillance and prevention efforts for vertical transmission of hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis in Nigeria and similar sub-Saharan African countries.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The models were calibrated using available epidemiologic literature and expert opinion, which may introduce uncertainty, and the evidence is based on projections rather than direct observational data, resulting in moderate confidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness of an integrated antenatal care testing panel for accelerating the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B in Nigeria. The panel, which tests for these infections with one finger prick, was found to avert 562 of the current 3,299 vertical infections per 100,000 women in antenatal care and reduce disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) at a net cost of US$7.55 per woman. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is $115 per DALY averted, more favorable than Nigeria's historical average. The study highlights the potential value of the panel in improving public health outcomes and suggests piloting in Nigeria to refine parameters for scale-up. However, the models rely on epidemiologic literature and expert opinion, which may introduce uncertainty, limiting the strength of the evidence to moderate.

analysis.scope_and_question: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) was initially developed to detect chromosomal abnormalities in fetuses through the analysis of cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood. Recent advancements have expanded NIPT's applications to include the detection of viral infections during pregnancy.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This study explores the clinical relevance of hepatitis B virus (HBV) cf-DNA using a dataset of approximately 500,000 NIPT visits and an independent validation cohort of 582 pregnant women (40 HBV-infected), aligned with HBV epidemiology from both population and individual perspectives.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Our analysis reveals that HBV cf-DNA is a strong biomarker of high viral infectivity rather than a general marker of infection, suggesting its potential to identify pregnant women at heightened risk of vertical transmission by the end of the first trimester.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Additionally, HBV-positive women showed a small but consistent reduction in fetal fraction relative to HBV-negative women across gestational weeks 9 - 17, an association compatible with an early effect of HBV on the placental contribution to cell-free DNA, although the observational design and unmeasured maternal covariates preclude causal inference.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The study suggests that HBV cf-DNA could be used to identify pregnant women at heightened risk of vertical transmission by the end of the first trimester, which may inform targeted interventions and surveillance strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the clinical relevance of hepatitis B virus (HBV) cell-free DNA (cf-DNA) in non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) as an early biomarker of viral infectivity. The study uses a large dataset of approximately 500,000 NIPT visits and an independent validation cohort of 582 pregnant women to assess HBV cf-DNA as a marker of high viral infectivity. The findings suggest that HBV cf-DNA may be a strong indicator of vertical transmission risk by the end of the first trimester, although the observational design limits causal inference. The study highlights the potential for using HBV cf-DNA in targeted prenatal screening and surveillance strategies to identify at-risk pregnant women.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the risk of hepatitis B virus reactivation in patients with HBsAg and HBV DNA double-negative lymphoma, addressing a gap in understanding how treatment duration and patient characteristics might influence this risk.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This correction addresses errors in the original study, which examined HBV reactivation in lymphoma patients undergoing treatment. The study population included patients with HBsAg and HBV DNA double-negative status, with treatment durations spanning different intervals.
analysis.methods: The study used a retrospective analysis of patient data, including treatment duration and HBV reactivation status. Statistical methods were employed to compare reactivation rates across different treatment periods and patient demographics.
analysis.main_results: No statistically significant differences in HBV reactivation rates were observed between genders (P = 0.637, OR = 0.855) or across varying treatment durations (P = 0.837). Additionally, patients with treatment durations exceeding 30 months were excluded from intergroup comparisons due to small sample sizes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that treatment duration does not significantly affect HBV reactivation rates in this specific patient population, highlighting the need for careful data interpretation in similar studies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide important insights for monitoring HBV reactivation in lymphoma patients, particularly those with HBsAg and HBV DNA double-negative status, and may inform future surveillance and diagnostic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include small sample sizes for certain treatment duration groups, which may affect the strength of conclusions. The evidence is moderate due to these constraints and the focus on a specific patient subset.

analysis.summary_en: This study corrects errors in the original analysis of HBV reactivation in lymphoma patients who are HBsAg and HBV DNA double-negative. It finds no significant differences in reactivation rates based on gender or treatment duration, with the exception of small sample sizes in longer treatment periods. The results suggest that treatment duration may not be a critical factor in HBV reactivation for this group, offering insights for clinical monitoring and future research. However, the study's conclusions are limited by its design and sample size, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection from serologic recovery in a patient with concurrent leptospirosis, a co-infection scenario with overlapping clinical features.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The paper presents a single-patient case report from a clinical setting, detailing the diagnostic workup and clinical course of a patient with suspected acute HBV infection during serologic recovery.
analysis.methods: The authors describe clinical evaluation, serologic testing for HBV markers (including HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, and anti-HBs), and laboratory confirmation of leptospirosis via serology or culture, alongside patient management and follow-up.
analysis.main_results: The patient exhibited serologic evidence of HBV recovery (anti-HBs positivity) with concurrent leptospirosis, demonstrating that acute HBV infection can be misdiagnosed in the context of co-infection due to overlapping clinical and laboratory findings.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the case as highlighting the diagnostic pitfalls of HBV serology during co-infection, emphasizing the need for careful interpretation of HBV markers in patients with febrile illnesses and potential leptospirosis exposure.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution clinicians to consider co-infections such as leptospirosis when interpreting HBV serology in patients with acute febrile illness, particularly in endemic regions, to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: As a single-case report, the evidence is limited in generalizability and cannot establish causality or prevalence; the strength of evidence is low due to the lack of comparative data or broader validation.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a patient with serologic evidence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) recovery (anti-HBs positivity) who presented with clinical features suggestive of acute HBV infection during concurrent leptospirosis. The authors emphasize the diagnostic challenge posed by overlapping clinical and laboratory findings in co-infection scenarios, where acute HBV infection may be misdiagnosed. The report underscores the need for clinicians to consider alternative diagnoses such as leptospirosis when interpreting HBV serology in patients with acute febrile illness, particularly in endemic settings. However, as a single-case report, the findings are not generalizable, and the evidence strength is low due to the absence of comparative data or broader validation.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the biogenesis and molecular characteristics of serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) RNA, focusing on the integrity and presentation of experimental data in previously published figures. It aimed to correct errors in specific panels and clarify methodological details to ensure accurate interpretation of HBV RNA biology.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The correction notice pertains to a previously published experimental study involving HBV genotypes B and E, patient sera, and HepAD38/HepDES19 cell lines. Original images underlying key panels (Figs 2A, 3A, 5B, S6B, S9A) and quantitative data (Figs 9, S9) were re-examined and corrected.
analysis.methods: Serum RNA from HBV-infected patients and cell supernatants was treated with NP40 and MNase or DNase I, followed by co-purification of viral DNA/RNA and analysis via Southern and Northern blotting. RT-PCR and electrophoresis were used to assess RNA integrity, with splice lines indicating gel lane adjustments for qualitative comparison.
analysis.main_results: The authors identified and corrected errors in Figs 3A and S9A, including overlapping rRNA panels and misaligned RNA/DNA capsid panels. Vertical discontinuities in Figs 5B and S6B were addressed by providing corrected versions with splice lines. Original underlying blot images and quantitative data were provided as supplementary files.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The correction underscores the importance of data integrity in experimental virology, particularly for HBV RNA studies. It highlights the need for rigorous figure assembly and transparency in presenting experimental results, though it does not introduce new biological findings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The correction ensures the reliability of previously reported HBV RNA data, which is critical for ongoing research on HBV replication and pathogenesis. Accurate representation of experimental results supports reproducibility and trust in scientific literature.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to a correction notice addressing figure errors and methodological clarifications, with no new experimental data or results. The strength of the evidence is moderate, as it relies on the integrity of the original study's methods and the authors' acknowledgment of errors.

analysis.summary_en: This correction notice addresses errors in previously published figures and methodological details from a study on the biogenesis and molecular characteristics of serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) RNA. The authors identified and corrected overlapping panels in Figs 3A and S9A, as well as vertical discontinuities in Figs 5B and S6B, providing revised versions with splice lines for clarity. Original underlying blot images and quantitative data were re-examined and made available as supplementary files. The notice emphasizes the importance of data integrity and transparency in experimental virology, particularly for HBV RNA research. While no new biological findings are presented, the correction ensures the reliability of previously reported data, supporting reproducibility and trust in the scientific literature.

The prevalence rate in the general population ranges between 8% and 12%, while among pregnant women, it is between 6.7% and 12.6%. The virus causes both acute and chronic disease, leading to severe health outcomes such as cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Annually, around 2,200 new liver cancer cases are linked to chronic hepatitis B, with late-stage survival rates under 5%. The economic burden is estimated at over $100 million annually in direct medical costs and lost productivity. In response, the government has reduced treatment costs through the Global Fund’s Pooled Procurement Mechanism, and health authorities are advocating for mass screening, childhood vaccination, and public education to address the crisis. These efforts aim to prevent further infections and reduce the long-term health and economic impact of the disease.

analysis.time: Published 17 August 2026; event described as ongoing with historical context from youth in northwestern Kenya.
analysis.location_and_population: Kenya, with regional focus on Turkana and Baringo counties; affected population includes mothers and infants in high-prevalence areas and general population unaware of HBV status.
analysis.event: Missiani Ochwoto, a senior virologist at KEMRI, leads Kenya's fight against hepatitis B as a personal crusade following the loss of a neighbor's family to HBV; the article profiles his advocacy, research, and prevention efforts.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: National HBV prevalence ~3.5% (~1 million infected); regional prevalence up to 7.6% in Turkana and Baringo; globally 254 million chronic HBV cases and up to 1.2 million deaths annually; HBV is second leading cause of cancer deaths in Kenya; 90% risk of chronic infection if infants contract HBV at birth; underfunding relative to HIV, TB, and malaria.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: KEMRI-led pilot programs in Baringo County show success in preventing mother-to-child transmission via birth-dose vaccination and antiviral treatment; expansion of point-of-care diagnostics and stigma reduction are ongoing priorities; policymaker funding allocation and infrastructure upgrades remain under-investigated and unresolved.

analysis.brief_en: Dr. Missiani Ochwoto, a senior virologist at Kenya’s Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), has transformed personal tragedy into a national crusade against hepatitis B. After witnessing a neighbor’s family succumb to the virus in northwestern Kenya, he dedicated his career to combating HBV, which infects roughly one million Kenyans and causes up to 1.2 million global deaths annually. Ochwoto champions the birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours of birth and antiviral treatment for HBV-positive mothers, with pilot programs in Baringo County showing zero transmission to newborns. Yet, rural diagnostic gaps and pervasive stigma—comparable to HIV—continue to obstruct progress. Despite WHO’s 2030 elimination target, Ochwoto warns that underfunding and weak infrastructure threaten Kenya’s ability to break transmission chains and save lives.
